note: Typical mistakes are tendencies, not rules about people. They happen because your first language has different sounds, letters or rules: this is called transfer (or interference). Not everyone makes these mistakes, and many learners stop making them quite quickly. If you know where a mistake comes from, you get rid of it faster. Based on comparing the language systems (contrastive linguistics) and on experience from language teaching.

languages.name: English
strengths: English and Spanish share thousands of words from Latin: hospital, animal, importante, familia.
English has the th of “think”, so the /θ/ of Spain (gracias, cerveza) isn't new to you.

mistakes.wrong: pero, perro with an English r (tongue curled back)
mistakes.right: pero: one tap · perro: several taps
mistakes.why: English r doesn't touch the top of the mouth. Spanish r does: one quick tap for r, a little like the tt in American “butter”, and several for rr.

mistakes.right: no, teléfono: every vowel short and clear
mistakes.why: In English, weak syllables turn into a short “uh” (/ə/), and many vowels glide. Spanish vowels keep their full sound in every syllable.
At the start of a word, English p, t, k come with a puff of air. Spanish p, t, k have none, so the puff sounds foreign straight away.

mistakes.wrong: vino, nuevo with top teeth on the bottom lip
mistakes.why: English has a separate v sound. Spanish doesn't: b and v are one sound, made with the lips only.

mistakes.wrong: “cara” for cada, “toro” for todo (a quick tap)
mistakes.right: cada, todo: soft d, like th in “this”
mistakes.why: Between vowels, English d is often a quick tap, and to Spanish ears that is an r. Spanish d there is soft, like th in “this”.

mistakes.wrong: zapato, plaza with a buzzing z
mistakes.right: zapato, plaza: /θ/ as in “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: English z buzzes, but Spanish has no such sound. In most of Spain z is /θ/, in Latin America and much of the south it is s. Both are correct; the buzz isn't.

mistakes.wrong: hola, hotel, hospital with a breath at the start
mistakes.why: English h is a breath. Spanish h is silent.
English says I am 25. Spanish says I have 25 years: tengo 25 años.
gustar works the other way round: literally, coffee pleases me. It's the same with encantar and doler.
English has one verb, to be. Spanish has two: ser for what you are, estar for where you are and how you are now.
In English the adjective comes first. In Spanish it usually comes after the noun, and agrees with it.

mistakes.right: Veo a Ana. Llamo a mi madre.
mistakes.why: When the object is a specific person, Spanish puts a in front. English has nothing like it.

mistakes.wrong: Espero por el autobús. Busco por las llaves.
mistakes.right: Espero el autobús. Busco las llaves.
mistakes.why: wait for and look for have a preposition in English. esperar and buscar don't need one.

mistakes.wrong: Estoy muy embarazada: he dicho una tontería.
mistakes.right: Estoy muy avergonzada: he dicho una tontería.
mistakes.why: False friend: embarazada = pregnant. More of them: éxito = success, carpeta = folder, constipado = with a cold, actualmente = at the moment.

mistakes.wrong: Cómo estás? Hablo Inglés los Lunes.
mistakes.why: Questions and exclamations open with ¿ and ¡. Languages, days and months take a small letter.

languages.name: German
strengths: Spanish verbs change for the person, as German ones do: ich gehe, du gehst – voy, vas.
You already know the difference between du and Sie: tú and usted work in much the same way.
Nouns with a gender aren't new to you, and Spanish has only two.

mistakes.right: zapato, cine: /θ/ as in English “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: German z is ts, and so is c in words like Celsius. Spanish has no ts here: in most of Spain it is /θ/, in Latin America and much of the south s.
German v is f or v, and w is v. Spanish b and v are one sound, made with the lips only: vino starts like Bein.

mistakes.wrong: sopa, museo with a buzzing s
mistakes.right: sopa, museo: always a sharp s
mistakes.why: German s before a vowel often buzzes (Sonne, Rose). Spanish s doesn't: it is the sharp s of das.

mistakes.wrong: pero, perro with an r in the throat
mistakes.right: pero: one tap · perro: several taps
mistakes.why: Most German r sounds are made in the throat, or disappear at the end of a word (Vater). Spanish r is made with the tongue tip, and you always hear it.
German p, t, k come with a puff of air. Spanish p, t, k have none.

mistakes.wrong: mi |amigo, en |España (a small stop before the vowel)
mistakes.why: German starts a word on a vowel with a small stop in the throat (Knacklaut). Spanish lets words run together.

mistakes.right: Madrid, ciudad, usted: a very soft d
mistakes.why: In German, d at the end of a word becomes t (Hund). In Spanish it stays very soft, close to th in English “this”.

mistakes.wrong: hola, hora with a breath at the start
mistakes.why: German h at the start of a word is a breath. Spanish h is silent.

mistakes.wrong: Mi hija estudia en el gimnasio.
mistakes.right: Mi hija estudia en el instituto.
mistakes.why: False friend: Gymnasium = instituto, and el gimnasio is a gym. More of them: Tasse = la taza (la tasa is a fee), Mantel = el abrigo (el mantel is a tablecloth), Regal = la estantería (el regalo is a present).
German says ich bin 30. Spanish uses tener: tengo 30 años.
German has one verb, sein. Spanish uses estar for where you are and how you are now, and ser for what you are.

mistakes.wrong: Ayer he trabajado hasta las seis.
mistakes.why: German uses the Perfekt for most things in the past. In Spain, a finished time (ayer, la semana pasada, en 2019) takes the indefinido.
A gender in German tells you nothing here. die Sonne and der Mond are the other way round in Spanish, so learn each noun with el or la.

mistakes.wrong: En Verano hablo Español con mis Amigos.
mistakes.right: En verano hablo español con mis amigos.
mistakes.why: German writes every noun with a capital. Spanish uses capitals only for names and at the start of a sentence.

languages.name: French
strengths: French and Spanish come from Latin and share a lot of grammar: gender, articles, the past tenses and the subjunctive.
Many words are close: famille – familia, université – universidad, liberté – libertad.

mistakes.wrong: pero, perro with a French r in the throat
mistakes.right: pero: one tap · perro: several taps
mistakes.why: French r is made in the throat. Spanish r is made with the tip of the tongue, behind the top teeth.

mistakes.wrong: pan, bien, tiempo with a French nasal vowel
mistakes.why: In French, n or m after a vowel often makes the vowel nasal and is not said itself. Spanish vowels stay clean, and you say the n or m.

mistakes.wrong: tú, luna, música with the French u of “tu”
mistakes.right: tú, luna, música: u like French “ou”
mistakes.why: French has two sounds here. Spanish u is always the “ou” of vous.

mistakes.right: teléfono, médico: stress on the accent
mistakes.why: French stresses the end of a word or phrase. Spanish stress can fall on different syllables, and moving it can change the word: hablo, habló.

mistakes.wrong: jamón, gente with the soft j of “je”
mistakes.right: jamón, gente: a rasp at the back of the mouth
mistakes.why: French j and ge are soft. Spanish j and ge are a rasp, close to the French r.

mistakes.wrong: casa, mesa with a buzzing s
mistakes.right: casa, mesa: always a sharp s
mistakes.why: In French, s between vowels buzzes (maison, rose). Spanish s doesn't.
French ch is sh. Spanish ch starts with the tongue touching the roof of the mouth, like tch in “tchèque”.

mistakes.wrong: Quité Francia en 2020. Atiendo el autobús.
mistakes.right: Dejé Francia en 2020. Espero el autobús.
mistakes.why: False friends: quitter = dejar (quitar is to remove), attendre = esperar (atender is to look after). Also: large = ancho, because largo means long.
French uses the passé composé for finished events. In Spain, a finished time (ayer, el lunes pasado) takes the indefinido.

mistakes.wrong: Yo hablo español y yo vivo en Madrid.
mistakes.right: Hablo español y vivo en Madrid.
mistakes.why: French always needs je. In Spanish the ending shows the person, so yo is only for emphasis.
French needs du, de la. Spanish has no partitive article: quiero pan, bebo agua.
French says depuis deux semaines. Spanish says llevo dos semanas aquí, or estoy aquí desde hace dos semanas.
Many genders are the same as in French, but not all: la couleur, le lait. Others are la nariz and el coche.
French has è and à. Spanish has only one written accent, the acute: á, é, í, ó, ú.

languages.name: Portuguese
strengths: Portuguese and Spanish share most of their everyday words: casa, mesa, família, trabalho – trabajo.
Portuguese nh (banho) is the same sound as Spanish ñ (baño).

mistakes.right: poco, noche, mesa: clear o, e, a
mistakes.why: Portuguese weakens vowels that aren't stressed: final o and e become u and i in Brazil, and nearly vanish in Portugal. Spanish vowels stay clear.

mistakes.wrong: jamón, gente with the soft Portuguese j
mistakes.right: jamón, gente: a rasp at the back of the mouth
mistakes.why: Portuguese j and ge are soft, as in “gente”. Spanish j and ge are a rasp, like ch in Scottish “loch”.

mistakes.right: carro, rojo: taps of the tongue tip
mistakes.why: Portuguese r at the start of a word and rr are often made in the throat, or sound like h in much of Brazil. Spanish rr and first r are several taps of the tongue tip.

mistakes.wrong: casa, mesa with a buzzing s; “dosh” for dos
mistakes.right: casa, mesa, dos: always a sharp s
mistakes.why: In Portuguese, s between vowels buzzes, and in Portugal and Rio a final s sounds like sh. Spanish s is the sharp s of “sol”.
Portuguese makes vowels nasal before n and m, and in ã and õ. Spanish vowels stay clean, and you say the n or m.
Portuguese ch is sh (chave). Spanish ch is the sound of tch in “tchau”.
Portuguese doesn't write ll, so it looks like a plain l. In most of Spain it sounds like y.

mistakes.wrong: Una ración de polvo, por favor.
mistakes.right: Una ración de pulpo, por favor.
mistakes.why: False friend: polvo = el pulpo (el polvo is dust). More of them: oficina = el taller, esquisito = raro, borracha = la goma, rato = el ratón.
Portuguese says eu gosto de café. In Spanish, gustar works the other way round: the thing pleases you.
Portuguese muito does both jobs. Spanish uses muy before an adjective and mucho before a noun or after a verb.
Portuguese can say o meu carro. In Spanish, mi, tu and su never come after an article.
Brazilian Portuguese says tem um bar. To say something exists, Spanish uses hay.
Portuguese builds compound tenses with ter (tinha comido). Spanish always uses haber: he comido, has ido.
Many genders are the same, but not all: a viagem, o sangue. Words in -aje are masculine in Spanish.
Portuguese -ção is usually -ción, and nh is ñ. Spanish doesn't use ç or ã.

languages.name: Italian
strengths: Italian and Spanish share a lot of vocabulary: casa, amico – amigo, libro.
Like Spanish, Italian usually leaves out the subject: parlo – hablo.

mistakes.right: cena, zapato: /θ/ as in English “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: In Italian, c before e, i is the sound of “cena”, and z is ts or dz. In Spanish, in most of Spain, both are /θ/; in Latin America and much of the south, s.

mistakes.right: gente, trabajo: a rasp at the back of the mouth
mistakes.why: Italian g before e, i is soft. Spanish g before e, i, and j, are a rasp, like ch in Scottish “loch”.
Italian has long consonants. Spanish doesn't, and many similar words are written with one consonant.

mistakes.wrong: pollo, calle with a long l, as in “bello”
mistakes.why: Italian ll is a long l. Spanish ll is another sound: in most of Spain, y.
Italian ch is k (chiesa). Spanish ch is the sound Italian writes c before e, i.

mistakes.wrong: casa, mesa with a buzzing s
mistakes.right: casa, mesa: always a sharp s
mistakes.why: In much of northern Italy, s between vowels buzzes. Spanish s doesn't.

mistakes.wrong: vino, nuevo with top teeth on the bottom lip
mistakes.why: Italian has a separate v sound. Spanish b and v are one sound, made with the lips only.

mistakes.wrong: Pan con burro. Salgo al tercer piso.
mistakes.right: Pan con mantequilla. Subo al tercer piso.
mistakes.why: False friends: burro = la mantequilla (el burro is a donkey), salire = subir (salir is to go out). Also: guardare = ver, largo = ancho, caldo = caliente.
Italian makes this tense with essere for many verbs: sono andato. Spanish always uses haber: he ido, he llegado.
Italian says sono stanco. Spanish uses estar for how you are now.
Italian uses the passato prossimo for many finished events. In Spain, a finished time (ayer, el año pasado) takes the indefinido.
Italian says la mia macchina. In Spanish, mi, tu and su never come after an article.
Italian makes plurals with -e and -i. Spanish adds -s or -es.
Italian writes many double letters. In Spanish the common ones are rr, ll and cc (acción).

languages.name: Romanian
strengths: Romanian is a Romance language too, and many words are close: casă – casa, carne – carne, apă – agua.
The verb ending shows the person, so you can leave out the subject, as in Spanish: vorbesc – hablo.
You say I like something the same way: îmi place cafeaua – me gusta el café.

mistakes.wrong: He comprado una carta en la librería.
mistakes.right: He comprado un libro en la librería.
mistakes.why: False friend: Romanian carte = el libro, and la carta is a letter. Also: larg = ancho, because largo means long.
Romanian adds the article to the end of the word: omul. In Spanish it's a separate word in front: el hombre.
Romanian has one verb, a fi. Spanish uses estar for where you are and how you are now, and ser for what you are.
Romanian uses the perfect compus for finished events. In Spain, a finished time (ayer, el año pasado) takes the indefinido.
Romanian says vreau să merg. When both verbs have the same person, Spanish uses the infinitive.

languages.name: Arabic
strengths: Spanish has thousands of words from Arabic: aceite, azúcar, almohada, ojalá.
Nouns have a gender, and the adjective usually comes after the noun: casa blanca.
The verb form shows the person, so you can often leave out the subject, as in Spanish.

mistakes.right: pero, pan: p without the voice
mistakes.why: Standard Arabic has no p, so it often becomes b. Put your fingers on your throat: for p nothing shakes until the vowel.

mistakes.right: mesa and misa, lona and luna: different words
mistakes.why: Arabic has three vowels (a, i, u), short or long. Spanish e and o lie between them, so they are easy to mix up.

mistakes.wrong: hola, hora with a clear ه
mistakes.why: Arabic h is always said. Spanish h is silent.

mistakes.wrong: hola, me llamo ana y vivo en madrid.
mistakes.right: Hola, me llamo Ana y vivo en Madrid.
mistakes.why: Arabic script has no capital and small letters. In Spanish, names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter.

mistakes.wrong: Mi hermano médico. Yo en Madrid.
mistakes.right: Mi hermano es médico. Estoy en Madrid.
mistakes.why: In the present, Arabic usually leaves out the verb be. Spanish needs ser or estar.
An Arabic relative clause repeats the thing with a pronoun. In standard Spanish it isn't repeated.
Genders often differ: in Arabic the sun is feminine and the moon masculine. Learn each Spanish noun with el or la.

languages.name: Russian
strengths: Nouns have a gender and verbs change for the person, so neither idea is new to you.
Like Spanish, Russian uses a double negative: я ничего не знаю – no sé nada.

mistakes.why: In Russian, o without stress sounds like a, and e like i. Spanish vowels keep their sound in every syllable.

mistakes.wrong: vino, nuevo with top teeth on the bottom lip (в)
mistakes.why: Russian в is a separate sound. Spanish b and v are one sound, made with the lips only.

mistakes.wrong: zapato, plaza with a buzzing з
mistakes.right: zapato, plaza: /θ/ as in English “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: Russian has no /θ/, and the letter z suggests з. In most of Spain z is /θ/, in Latin America and much of the south s. Both are correct; the buzz isn't.

mistakes.right: El libro está en la mesa.
mistakes.why: Russian has no articles. A Spanish noun usually needs one, with the right gender.
In the present, Russian leaves out the verb be (Я студент). Spanish needs ser or estar.
Russian doesn't separate these two ideas. For a place, use estar: estoy en casa, está en Madrid.
Russian shows the object with an ending (Анну). Spanish puts a in front of a person.
In Russian the adjective comes first. In Spanish it usually comes after the noun.

languages.name: Ukrainian
strengths: Nouns have a gender and verbs change for the person, so neither idea is new to you.
A yes/no question can be made with the voice alone, as in Spanish: Ти хочеш чаю? – ¿Quieres té?

mistakes.right: gato, amigo: g as in ґ
mistakes.why: Ukrainian г is a breathy sound, close to h. Spanish g is closer to ґ, and softer between vowels.

mistakes.wrong: vino, nuevo with the sound of в
mistakes.why: Ukrainian в is a separate sound. Spanish b and v are one sound, made with the lips only.

mistakes.wrong: zapato, plaza with a buzzing з
mistakes.right: zapato, plaza: /θ/ as in English “think” (or s in the south)
mistakes.why: Ukrainian has no /θ/, and the letter z suggests з. In most of Spain z is /θ/, in Latin America and much of the south s. Both are correct; the buzz isn't.

mistakes.right: La mesa está en la cocina.
mistakes.why: Ukrainian has no articles. A Spanish noun usually needs one, with the right gender.
In the present, Ukrainian usually leaves out the verb be (Я вчителька). Spanish needs ser or estar.
Ukrainian doesn't separate these two ideas. For a place, use estar.
Ukrainian shows the object with an ending. Spanish puts a in front of a person.

languages.name: Chinese
strengths: Like Spanish, Chinese puts the subject first, then the verb, then the object: 我喝咖啡 – Yo bebo café.
Chinese often leaves out I when it's clear, and Spanish does that all the time.

mistakes.right: pero and pelo, hora and hola: different words
mistakes.why: Mandarin has no tapped r, and r and l are easy to mix up. For l the tongue stays up; for r it taps once and goes.

mistakes.wrong: pan with a puff of air, bueno without any voice
mistakes.right: pan: no puff · bueno: voice on from the start
mistakes.why: Mandarin tells b and p apart by a puff of air. Spanish tells them apart by the voice: p has no puff, b has voice.

mistakes.right: hablar, mal: say the last sound
mistakes.why: Mandarin syllables end almost only in n, ng or a vowel. Spanish words often end in s, l, r or d, and the ending carries meaning.
Mandarin syllables don't start with two consonants, so a vowel slips in. Spanish has many: pl-, tr-, gr-, fr-.
Chinese verbs never change. Spanish verbs change for the person: trabajo, trabajas, trabaja.
Chinese nouns have no plural and no gender. In Spanish, nouns and adjectives show both, and they must agree.
Chinese shows time with words like yesterday (昨天). Spanish changes the verb too: voy → fui.

mistakes.right: El libro está en la mesa.
mistakes.why: Chinese has no articles. A Spanish noun usually needs one.
In Chinese the place comes before the verb (我在马德里工作). In Spanish it usually comes after.

quiz.prompt: Why do many learners with Arabic as their first language write names with a small letter?
options: Their script has no capital letters
In Arabic everything is written in capitals
quiz.answer: Their script has no capital letters
quiz.explain: In Spanish, names and the first word of a sentence start with a capital letter.

quiz.prompt: How do you say your age correctly?
quiz.explain: Soy 25 años comes from English or German. Spanish uses tener.
A false friend for speakers of English, Portuguese, Italian and French. Embarrassed: avergonzado/a.

quiz.prompt: You moved here three years ago and you still live here. What is correct?
quiz.explain: A length of time still going on: llevo tres años aquí, or estoy aquí desde hace tres años.

quiz.prompt: You like books. What do you say?
quiz.explain: gustar agrees with the thing you like. Yo gusto comes from English or Portuguese.

quiz.prompt: Where does the adjective usually go in Spanish?
options: At the end of the sentence
quiz.explain: una casa blanca, un coche nuevo.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between pero and perro?
options: One tap of the tongue or several
quiz.answer: One tap of the tongue or several
quiz.explain: pero has one quick tap, and perro has several. They are different words.

quiz.prompt: You feel cold. What do you say?
quiz.explain: How your body feels goes with tener. It's the same in French (j'ai froid), Italian (ho freddo) and Portuguese (tenho frio).

quiz.prompt: What is el gimnasio in Spain?
quiz.explain: A false friend for German speakers: das Gymnasium = el instituto.
